messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Tran, a 69-year-old widowed man of South Eastern Asian descent, has been a dedicated nanny to his grandchildren since his wife passed away five years ago. His life took an unexpected and tragic turn when one of his beloved grandsons fell severely ill with a life-threatening condition that nearly claimed the child’s life. The memory of that time is seared into Mr. Tran's mind; it feels more real than any ordinary experience he has had. He struggles to articulate what happened even to himself, but the vividness of the event haunts him daily. The memories do not feel like they belong in the past—they feel as though they are happening right now, each moment replaying in his mind with stark clarity. Mr. Tran’s interpretation of this experience has led him to distrust others deeply. He feels that people are not what they seem, and he is certain that the trauma has permanently changed him for the worse. This belief that he has become an unrecognizable person has driven him to avoid medical care or psychological help. Seeking such assistance only serves as a painful reminder of his perceived failures during that critical time. He tries hard not to think about what happened, but when memories inevitably intrude, they feel overwhelmingly present and real, making it difficult for him to distinguish between the past and the present. This difficulty has led Mr. Tran to keep himself occupied all the time, distracting himself with any activity that might temporarily alleviate the overwhelming presence of these memories. His occupation as a nanny has become a double-edged sword. While he finds solace in caring for his grandchildren, it also serves as a constant reminder of the child who nearly died. He fears that by not being vigilant enough or by seeking help, something similar could happen again. This fear exacerbates his avoidance behaviors and distracts him from fully engaging with those around him. Mr. Tran’s struggle has taken a toll on his relationships, particularly with his family members who have noticed his increasing isolation and reluctance to discuss the past. His attempts at mental distraction have led to periods of exhaustion, further deepening his sense of disconnection and self-doubt. The cycle is tightening; as he avoids seeking medical or psychological help, the vividness of his memories increases, reinforcing his negative appraisals about himself and others. He feels trapped in a world where the trauma continues to define him, and each attempt at distraction only serves to highlight the very thing he fears most—his unrecognizable self. What finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was a recent health scare of his own that forced him to confront the fact that avoiding medical care could have dire consequences. He is most afraid of feeling perpetually trapped by the trauma, but he also hopes for a chance to reclaim a sense of normalcy and connection with those around him.
